title: Audit storage slicing and backfill + pipeline observability notes
summary: Working notes on a sliced retention model for audit events, implementation options for indexing and backfills, observable failure modes, and quick runbook actions. Focused on bridging audit storage economics with SIEM export reliability and RBAC-v2 access controls.
content:
Purpose:
This doc captures an implementation approach for audit event storage slicing (hot/warm/cold/archive), concrete indexing strategies to support fast forensics and SIEM exports, a pragmatic backfill plan for missed partitions, and the observable failure modes that we should monitor. It is intentionally operational — mixing design constraints, cost tradeoffs, and specific runbook steps.

Scope / assumptions:
- Source of truth for events is the ingestion Kafka topic (audit-events-prod).
- Downstream storage tiers: hot (Elasticsearch cluster A), warm (Elasticsearch cluster B), cold (object store: s3://redwood-audit-cold), archive (WORM vault).
- SIEM export (Splunk/Customer SIEM) pulls from a dedicated export service that reads from the hot/warm index layer and the object-store fallback for older ranges.
- RBAC v2 controls access at index and object prefix levels; key usage governed by KMS.
- We must support 90 days of nearline searchable events with sub-second to second query SLAs for forensics, and 1 year of low-cost retention for compliance review. Longer-term archives (3+ years) are WORM and offline retrieval.

Retention slicing model (proposal):
- T0 (hot): 0–7 days — full indexing at event level, complete parsed fields, denormalized user/service metadata, high-replication ES index. Purpose: live incident response, SIEM real-time export, fast audits.
- T1 (warm): 8–90 days — partial indexing: core fields (timestamp, actor_id, action, resource, outcome, correlation_id), compressed doc store, reduced replicas. Searchable but more limited (no large text blobs).
- T2 (cold): 91–365 days — events stored as compressed jsonl on object store with a compact index (daily shard manifest). Searches run as two-stage queries: index manifest -> object retrieval.
- T3 (archive): 366+ days — WORM snapshot, retrieval by e-Discovery only, 48–72 hour retrieval SLA.

Indexing strategy details:
- Schema: maintain canonical audit-schema v2 (schema version in each event). For T0 keep full schema; for T1/T2 store 'indexable' fields and a pointer to the raw payload in S3.
- Partition keys: daily time-based partitions (UTC) plus tenant hash for multi-tenant slicing. Index names: audit-events-YYYY.MM.DD-tenanthex.
- Primary keys: event_id (uuidv4) + ingestion_offset to avoid duplicates.
- Mapping choices: use keyword for actor_id/resource/action, date_nanos for timestamp to support high-qps. Avoid dynamic mapping for free text fields — use a 'raw_payload' binary pointer instead.
- Retention movement: a daily job (index-archiver) will reindex or export from T0->T1 and copy compressed jsonl from T1->T2, deleting heavy indices post-confirmation. Each archive action writes a tombstone record to a metadata index (audit-archival-manifest) for provenance.

Backfill and repair plan (missed partitions / ingestion gaps):
- Detection: consumer-lag monitors and the archive manifest comparator will surface gaps. A backfill candidate is any day where (expected_event_count - stored_event_count) > threshold (configurable per tenant).
- Sources for backfill: primary Kafka topic (retained for 30 days), local ingest buffer (7 days), backup object-store dump snapshots.
- Backfill modes:
  1) Fast reindex: stream from Kafka to a temporary ES ingest cluster, run validation, and perform atomic alias swap into T0/T1 for small gaps.
  2) Bulk reconstruct: for older gaps beyond Kafka retention, use object-store snapshots and run a bulk import pipeline that builds compact indices (T1) and then optionally rehydrates into T0 for high-priority tenants.
- Consistency: backfills must mark events with backfill_metadata (backfilled_by, backfill_run_id, original_ingest_timestamp) so downstream consumers and auditors can distinguish original vs backfilled records.

Failure modes and observable signals:
- Failure: indexer job crashes during reindex -> signal: incomplete alias update + index health changes + archive-manifest mismatch.
  Mitigation: alert to infra/eng on partial reindex, roll back alias, requeue daily job for retry; if repeated, escalate to SRE.
- Failure: ES cluster full / shard allocation errors -> signal: yellow/red cluster health, increased query latency, write errors in producer logs.
  Mitigation: automatic routing to warm/cold queues, throttle non-critical writes (metrics only), page on-call SRE runbook for shard rebalancing and emergency snapshot+restore to alternate cluster.
- Failure: object store write errors during T1->T2 copy -> signal: S3 5xx errors, archive-manifest missing entries for that date.
  Mitigation: exponential retry with jitter; if destination consistently fails, freeze retention movement for that tenant, surface to compliance team, trigger tmpr object-store bucket fallback (secondary region).
- Failure: SIEM export consumer falling behind -> signal: export-lag > SLA, retry queue growing, duplicate-export errors on replays.
  Mitigation: fall back to on-demand export from compressed daily manifests, notify CS/Customer about possible delivery delay; for high-severity data, rehydrate T0 slice for immediate pickup.

Monitoring and alerts (SLO-minded):
- Metrics to emit: ingest_rate, write_error_rate, consumer_lag_days, archive_manifest_mismatch_count, backfill_jobs_failed, avg_query_latency_7d.
- Alerts (examples):
  - P0: consumer_lag_days > 2 for top-tier tenants (paged immediately).
  - P1: archive_manifest_mismatch_count > 0 for 6 hours (channel + ticket).
  - P2: average_query_latency_7d above 2s for hot-index (email to infra).
- Dashboards: retention heatmap (per-tenant, per-day), backfill job status board, SIEM export throughput and error rates.

RBAC v2 implications (notes):
- Index-level ACLs: hot indices are accessible to SRE/IR teams; warm indices are restricted to compliance + auditors via temporary roles; cold object prefixes require KMS-wrapped access tokens and a separate KMS key per region.
- Principle of least privilege: SIEM-export service uses a dedicated service role with read-only access to T0/T1 indices and read list access to manifest objects. No single user/service should hold both archive-delete and archive-initiate capabilities.
- Audit trails: all index/delete/migration operations must themselves be logged as audit-events and appear in a protected index that is immutably replicated to the archive.

SIEM export integration model:
- Real-time export: tail T0 indices via change-stream connector to the SIEM ingest pipeline. This handles immediate alerting and security use cases.
- Bulk export: for daily deliveries, the export worker composes an export bundle from T1 manifest + raw payloads to guarantee completeness (used when the SIEM requests full-day replays).
- De-duplication: exports embed event_id + origin_offset, SIEM side should dedupe by these fields. Our export worker will attempt idempotent retries.

Cost and operational tradeoffs (brief):
- Full indexing of all fields for 90 days provides best UX but multiplies storage and ES CPU costs. The proposed hybrid model reduces ongoing ES footprint by ~45% (internal estimate) while keeping 7 day full searchability.
- Backfill-readiness requires maintaining Kafka retention and periodic snapshotting. Longer Kafka retention reduces backfill complexity but increases infra cost.

Minimal runbook snippets (for on-call):
- Problem: SIEM export stalled > 30m
  1) Check export-worker logs and export-lag metric.
  2) If lag caused by ES write errors, check ES cluster health and replica allocation.
  3) If lag caused by inability to read warm indices, try running on-demand daily-manifest export for affected date.
  4) Notify CS/affected-customer teams with ETA.

- Problem: Archive-manifest mismatch for 2025-02-10
  1) Query archive-manifest index for that date.
  2) Check object store for presence of s3://redwood-audit-cold/2025-02-10/*.gz.
  3) If missing, attempt quick recovery from backup bucket or request SRE snapshot restore.
  4) If full recovery not possible, prepare incident report and notify compliance with remediation plan.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Decide final TTL for Kafka topic (30 days vs 60 days) given backfill SLA targets. TODO: cost run that compares additional retention cost vs estimated backfill effort. (Owner: Noah)
- Define compact index schema for T1 (fields included/excluded). TODO: finalize list and benchmark 7/30/90 day query latencies. (Owner: Sofia)
- Build automated test harness that simulates lost partition and validates backfill paths. (Owner: Marcus)

Notes on uniqueness and auditability:
- Every retention action must insert a tombstone/manifest entry so audits can reconstruct exactly what was moved/deleted and by whom. Manifests are the single source-of-truth for retention movement decisions.
- Backfilled events must not be silently overridden — they should have a clear provenance field and a small UI flag in the security console.

Appendix: short checklist for a single-day retention move (operator):
- Verify index health and replicas for the date range in T0.
- Snapshot raw payloads to s3://redwood-audit-cold/pending/YYYY-MM-DD/ and confirm checksum.
- Write archive-manifest entry with checksums and counts.
- Update retention index (alias swap) and set TTL on T0 to trigger deletion after safe window.
- Validate SIEM-export sample for that date (compare counts).

End of notes.
